strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: manipulation of independently moving objects. DOMINO is ambitious in scale, containing 117K trajectories, 35 tasks, five embodiments, three motion-complexity levels, and paired static/dynamic settings.

Although no contribution type is declared, the work is best viewed as a hybrid Datasets/Benchmarks and Algorithms/General submission, with the benchmark as its primary contribution. This framing strengthens the significance of the broad task taxonomy, automated data-generation pipeline, and extensive per-task reporting.

PUMA is technically intuitive: compact optical-flow history supplies explicit motion cues, while object-centric future-feature prediction provides training-only anticipation supervision without increasing inference cost. The component study shows a consistent progression from 10.86% SR for the baseline to 11.71% with flow, 14.80% with future prediction, and 17.20% with a longer prediction horizon.

The empirical scope is strong. The paper evaluates numerous VLA baselines, reports 100 closed-loop episodes per task, includes complete task-level results, examines higher-order dynamics, history length, prediction horizon, data scaling, latency, and conducts physical-robot experiments.

PUMA produces meaningful gains on the principal Level-1 benchmark: 17.20% SR and 34.97 MS versus 10.86% and 30.49 for the strongest matched Qwen3-VL baseline. The real-robot result, averaging 42% success over five tasks compared with 24% for pi0.5, is also encouraging.

The paper is generally clear and visually polished, and the supplement documents training settings, trajectory generation, optical flow, grounding, and acknowledged limitations such as stop-on-contact dynamics and sim-to-real mismatch.
weaknesses: The benchmark construction creates a potentially consequential shortcut. Demonstrations are generated by first planning a static expert trajectory and then back-calculating an object trajectory so that the object reaches the preselected manipulation pose at the recorded execution time. The robot subsequently replays the static motion plan. Thus the demonstrations are synchronized open-loop replays rather than expert reactions to independently sampled motion, and motion, endpoint, and action timing are structurally correlated. The paper does not demonstrate that policies must infer dynamics rather than exploit task-specific timing or endpoint priors.

The central claim of generalizable dynamic manipulation is substantially broader than the evidence. Most results use the same 35 training tasks, one Aloha-AgileX embodiment, clean backgrounds, Level-1 motion, and alpha=0.1. Four advertised embodiments and domain-randomized data are not evaluated. Level-2/3 experiments use only ten tasks and include target-level training or LoRA adaptation, rather than zero-shot transfer to unseen dynamics, tasks, objects, or embodiments.

The claim that dynamic data fosters generalizable representations is overstated. Dynamic-to-static transfer is evaluated on static counterparts of the same tasks and is much worse on average than static training (for example, pi0.5 obtains 22.54% versus 44.83% SR). The discussion highlights selected favorable tasks. Co-training also adds data without a size-matched control, so its gain cannot be attributed specifically to complementary dynamic representations.

The proposed Manipulation Score is not convincingly valid across the diverse tasks. It measures final end-effector proximity to a target, uses the better arm in bimanual settings, and applies ad hoc multiplicative penalties. This can reward approach without successful grasping, handover, pressing, shaking, or placement. The stated range of RC is not reconciled with the presented formula, which can become negative or otherwise require unspecified clipping.

Ablations do not fully isolate the method's contributions. There is no future-prediction-only condition, no comparison with alternative motion representations or modern flow estimators, and no direct evaluation showing that the world queries actually predict object motion. The raw-frame baseline may also receive a substantially different token/input configuration. Consequently, the claimed necessity of jointly combining history and anticipation is not established.

No training-seed variation, confidence intervals, or significance analysis is reported. This matters for low success rates and especially for the real-world study, which uses only 20 trials per task. It is also unclear whether real-world baselines receive the same simulation initialization as PUMA, whose LoRA adaptation starts from a DOMINO-trained simulation checkpoint.

The dynamic-coefficient generalization experiment is internally ambiguous: training uses alpha=0.1, while the purported randomized test samples alpha from [0.5,1.5], implying speeds 5-15 times larger, yet the text describes this as ordinary variability and attributes success to proportional flow scaling. It may instead intend a multiplier range, but the benchmark definition and table do not say so.

The simulator stops autonomous object motion upon contact. While useful for interception, this weakens the claimed continuous-tracking setting and omits precisely the post-contact dynamics that make many dynamic manipulation tasks difficult. The physical experiments likewise use objects pulled along controlled linear paths and task-specific real demonstrations, providing limited evidence for unconstrained deployment.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the substantial supplement: important details such as flow thresholds, observation/control timing, exact train/evaluation trajectory splits, and several task-success specifications are absent. The project and code fields are blank in the submitted PDF, so actual release availability cannot be verified. There is also at least one inappropriate attribution: citation [60], a multimodal recommendation paper, is cited as prior dynamic-manipulation work.

strengths: Although no contribution type is declared, the work is best viewed primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution with an accompanying algorithm. Dynamic manipulation is important and comparatively underexplored, and DOMINO offers substantial scale: 117,000 trajectories, 35 tasks, five robot embodiments, paired static/dynamic settings, and three nominal motion-complexity levels.

The evaluation includes numerous VLA baselines, full per-task results, transfer experiments, component ablations, latency measurements, and a small real-robot study. This is broader than a purely proof-of-concept evaluation.

PUMA is a sensible engineering combination of compact optical-flow history and auxiliary object-centric future-feature prediction. It improves average Level-1 success from 10.86% for the matched Qwen3-VL OpenVLA-OFT implementation to 17.20%, without a substantial reported latency penalty.
The paper is generally organized clearly and candidly acknowledges low absolute success rates, simplified contact dynamics, sim-to-real limitations, and several recurring failure modes.
weaknesses: The benchmark evidence does not match its breadth of claims. Nearly all headline experiments use only one embodiment, clean backgrounds, Level-1 constant-velocity motion, and alpha=0.1. Level-2/3 evaluation is restricted to a selected 10-task subset, while domain-randomized and cross-embodiment policy evaluations are absent. Consequently, the claimed generalizable benchmark spanning five embodiments and hierarchical dynamics is not convincingly validated.

The data-generation design substantially simplifies the central problem. A static rollout first determines the robot execution time, after which the moving object's trajectory is back-calculated to reach the planned interaction point at that time; the object then stops autonomous motion upon contact. This produces synchronized demonstrations but largely avoids online interception planning and post-contact dynamics, limiting the realism and generality of conclusions about dynamic manipulation.

The proposed Manipulation Score is insufficiently justified and appears poorly aligned with many tasks. It measures final end-effector proximity to the target, takes the better arm for bimanual tasks, and assigns success a score of 100. This does not naturally measure progress for handover, shaking, scanning, pressing, or multi-stage placement, and no validation against task progress or human judgment is provided. Per-task success criteria and several penalty details are also underspecified.

The mechanism claimed for PUMA is not demonstrated. Masked average-pooled DINO features may predominantly encode object identity or appearance rather than future pose or motion; the paper provides no prediction-error analysis, representation probe, or controls using current-time, shuffled, or time-invariant feature targets. Thus the gains do not establish that the world queries actually forecast future object states.

The ablation is not fully factorial, and baseline fairness remains unclear. There is no auxiliary-prediction-only condition, no raw-history-only result in the main 35-task evaluation, and the strongest history-aware comparison is limited to 10 selected tasks. Several relevant temporal VLA methods discussed in related work are not evaluated. Baselines use differing original architectures or author reimplementations, while ACT is trained per task and VLAs jointly, complicating interpretation.

The generalization claim is overstated and partly contradicted by the reported averages. In dynamic-to-static transfer, dynamic-trained policies are substantially worse overall than static-trained counterparts: 13.97 vs. 27.74 for ACT, 14.09 vs. 17.51 for OpenVLA-OFT, and 22.54 vs. 44.83 for pi-0.5. The paper emphasizes selected favorable tasks instead. Co-training also adds data without an equal-data control, so its improvement does not show that dynamic data specifically creates better representations.

The real-robot evidence is small and confounded: five tasks with 20 trials each, string-driven linear object motion, and no uncertainty estimates or repeated training seeds. PUMA is LoRA-adapted from its simulation checkpoint, whereas equivalent simulation pretraining for every baseline is not established. This prevents attributing the 42% versus 24% result solely to the architecture.

Statistical reliability is not addressed anywhere: results are single point estimates without confidence intervals, seed variation, or significance testing. The alpha generalization experiment is also internally questionable: training uses alpha=0.1, yet the alleged randomized test samples alpha from [0.5,1.5], despite alpha being defined as maximum speed in m/s; this surprising regime and its results require clarification.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the large artifact contribution. The manuscript does not fully specify all 35 task success predicates, action execution/replanning details, synchronization and delay behavior, or training cost, and the displayed project/code fields provide no accessible resource. There is also at least one plainly mismatched citation: reference 60 is a multimodal recommendation paper cited as dynamic manipulation work. Overall, these concerns affect benchmark validity and the paper's main causal claims, rather than being minor presentation issues.

strengths: This is a timely and meaningful contribution to dynamic robotic manipulation. Although no contribution type is explicitly declared, I assess it primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks paper with an Algorithms/General component: DOMINO’s 117K trajectories, 35 tasks, five embodiments, two interaction categories, and three levels of motion complexity constitute the strongest part of the submission. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/f38aaa98abc149cc9b2f59a88dd23377/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The paper convincingly establishes that dynamic manipulation is not solved by existing static-task VLAs: representative models suffer large static-to-dynamic degradation, and fine-tuning on dynamic data provides only limited recovery. The paired static/dynamic task design helps isolate this effect.

PUMA is technically sensible and well aligned with the diagnosed problem. Optical-flow history supplies explicit motion evidence, while object-centric future-feature prediction encourages anticipation without adding the training-only prediction branch to inference.

The empirical coverage is unusually broad: numerous contemporary baselines, 100 evaluation episodes per task, task-type breakdowns, latency measurements, component and horizon ablations, cross-level and speed-shift tests, data-scaling analysis, and detailed per-task results.

The principal result is substantial: PUMA reaches 17.20% SR and 34.97 MS versus 10.86% and 30.49 for the strongest matched Qwen3-VL OpenVLA-OFT implementation. It also improves both interception and tracking tasks.
The five-task physical-robot study adds practical evidence: over 20 trials per task, PUMA averages 42% success versus 24% for π0.5, while operating at 9.6 Hz with latency comparable to π0.5.

The manuscript is clear and visually polished, provides extensive implementation details and dataset-format information, and candidly discusses failure modes and limitations such as stop-on-contact dynamics, control delay, data cost, and the sim-to-real gap.
weaknesses: The strongest claims of generalizable dynamic manipulation exceed the central evidence. Full-scale evaluation concentrates on clean Level-1 linear motion with one Aloha-AgileX embodiment; Level-2/3 experiments use only ten tasks, while cross-embodiment and domain-randomized results are not reported despite being prominent dataset features.

Absolute simulated performance remains low: PUMA succeeds on only 17.20% of Level-1 episodes, and Level-3 success is 4.6% on the ten-task subset. This supports the benchmark’s difficulty and the method’s relative improvement, but not yet robust dynamic manipulation.

The simulator simplifies the core physical challenge: targets are kinematic, demonstrations are produced by synchronizing replayed static motion plans, and autonomous object motion stops upon contact. Consequently, post-contact dynamics, target response to impacts, and genuinely reactive expert behavior are largely absent.

The Manipulation Score needs stronger validation. Its route-completion expression is stated to lie in [0,100] without an explicit clipping rule; taking the maximum progress of either arm can over-credit incomplete bimanual behavior; and the 0.5/0.8 penalties appear heuristic. Sensitivity analysis or correlation with human judgments would strengthen its standing as a benchmark metric.

The ablation does not include auxiliary future prediction without optical-flow history. It therefore cannot cleanly separate the auxiliary objective’s independent effect from its interaction with flow; notably, flow alone improves SR only from 10.86% to 11.71%, whereas most of the gain appears after adding prediction.

The real-world comparison has a potential training asymmetry: PUMA is initialized from its simulation checkpoint and adapted with LoRA, but it is unclear whether competing methods receive comparable simulation pretraining. Motion generated by pulling objects on transparent strings also covers only controlled linear dynamics.

Results appear to come from single training runs, with no across-seed variation or confidence intervals. Episode-level uncertainty alone would not capture training instability, which is important given the low success rates and several relatively small differences.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete for the optical-flow estimator and precise temporal sampling intervals. The manuscript’s Project Page and Code fields are also blank, so the promised release cannot presently be verified.
Table 14 labels its speed-randomization regime as α sampled from [0.5,1.5], despite training at α=0.1 and defining α in meters per second. This surprising range requires confirmation or correction.
